turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Vihaan is here, doctor. I just checked him outside, temperature is 38.9, pulse 132, oxygen saturation 97 percent, and his breathing rate is 28. He kept pushing the probe away.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Send the file through. Come, sit, sit. Tell me, what has been happening?
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, he is having fever, and cough also. He turned two last month. Since this started he is very irritable, not sleeping properly, not himself at all.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Both together. When did it actually start?
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): From three days... sorry, no. It started Thursday night, so that makes four days.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thursday? We were at my cousin's till Friday. The fever came Saturday morning, that is two days only.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hmm, you are not matching. I will not pick one of you. Somewhere between two and four days, and we leave the exact day open.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): At home last night the forehead thermometer showed one hundred and two... no, one hundred and three. Fahrenheit, I mean.
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That strip is not reliable. Under the arm, digital, it was 101, not more than that.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the height is also disputed, 103 versus 101, and I trust the 38.9 we just measured more than either home thermometer. Vihaan, beta, does your throat hurt?
[SEG0011] person_5 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He does, doctor. He has been pointing inside his mouth and he refused his biscuits. He said no only because he is fed up.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, throat pain is not agreed, I'll look myself. Is he drinking, and is urine coming?
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mm, I suppose... sometimes, not really. A sip, then he turns away. I can't say properly.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): That is a maybe, not a yes. I won't write down that he is dehydrated. Any vomiting, or loose stools?
[SEG0016] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He vomited once yesterday, just after that syrup we gave. Stools, sometimes, not really. Maybe one soft one. Nothing ongoing.
[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That was not vomit. He brought a little of the cetirizine back up, that is all. And stools are normal, he went this morning, normal only.

[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Vomiting is disputed then, one of you says once, the other says it was only a bit of syrup. I'll leave it unresolved. Loose stools I will take as not really there. What medicine has he actually had?
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Paracetamol syrup. I was calling it Crocin... actually the bottle is Calpol, same paracetamol. I gave 5 ml this morning.
[SEG0020] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Last night I was going to say 7.5... no, the spoon is 5 ml, one spoon. But you filled it twice, I saw, so it became 10 ml.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I did not. It was one 5 ml. You were on the phone.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Paracetamol is in use, but we do not have an agreed amount, 5 ml against about 10. How often has it been given?
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Every six hours, only when the fever is up. That part we both did.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did anyone give ibuprofen, or a cough syrup, or an antibiotic?
[SEG0025] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I bought Ibugesic syrup from the chemist, for the high fever. We never opened the seal. It is sitting in the bag, so he has not had any.
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yesterday I gave cetirizine syrup, 2.5 ml... no, sorry, the cup was the 5 ml one, once. He became very drowsy, so I stopped it. No antibiotic at all.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Cetirizine once, then stopped. Ibugesic never given, so it does not go on his medicines. And nothing antibiotic. The drowsiness settled after that?
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, by evening he was back to his usual irritable self, not that heavy sleep.

[SEG0029] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Also, don't mix up my bag, doctor. My father takes metformin, 500 milligrams, for his sugar. My sister's biotin gummies are in the same pouch. Those are hers, not for Vihaan.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Understood. Metformin and biotin belong to your father and your sister, not this child. So paternal grandfather has diabetes. I will note that. Any asthma in the family?
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): My mother has asthma, she uses a pump. We did not give him her inhaler, definitely not.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grandmother with asthma, noted, and her inhaler was not used. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. No allergies.
[SEG0034] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Last year, amoxicillin, he got red spots all over the tummy. We stopped it on day two. The ENT had given it for an ear infection.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That was a viral rash, the doctor said it at the time. He can take amoxicillin. It is not an allergy.

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I am hearing two stories, so the amoxicillin reaction stays disputed, not confirmed. We simply will not use amoxicillin today. Is the cough worse at night? Any breathlessness?
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Cough is more at night, dry cough. When he is sitting quietly he is not breathless, but when the fever spikes he breathes fast.
[SEG0038] person_5 (PATIENT): Mama... no.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He wants down from the chair. Sorry, doctor. One second. Okay, sit, beta.

[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me listen while he is still. Chest is clear on both sides, with no wheeze and no crackles. Throat is mildly red and the tonsils are not big. Both ears are fine, and the abdomen is soft with no guarding.
[SEG0041] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So you are thinking pneumonia or no?

[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): I am thinking, out loud, this is most likely a viral fever with a cough. An early chest infection is still possible, I cannot fully rule it out, but with a clear chest today it sits lower.

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Continue the paracetamol, but only to the 5 ml mark, that is 120 mg of the 120 mg per 5 ml syrup, every six hours if his temperature is 38 or above. Not a kitchen spoon, and do not add the Ibugesic unless we talk again.
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): 5 ml, 120 mg, six hourly with fever. I will hide the other bottle.
[SEG0045] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And cetirizine, should we repeat it at night for the cough?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, leave the cetirizine off. One dose made him drowsy and a dry cough will not settle with it.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Small sips of water often, even if he fusses. If he is breathing much faster, if the lips turn blue, or if urine stops, go to emergency. Do not wait for the review.
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): If lips are blue, emergency. Yes.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): No blood test today. If the fever has not settled in two days, then a full blood count, and I want to see him again.
[SEG0050] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So we come only if it is still there?
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. If it is not better in two days, blood count and a review with me. If he worsens tonight or tomorrow, you come earlier, you don't wait out the two days.
[SEG0052] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He is only asking for curd rice, nothing else. Is that a problem?
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): Curd rice is perfectly fine. Don't force a big meal while he is febrile.
[SEG0054] person_5 (PATIENT): Water.
[SEG0055] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): There, now he wants water. I have the bottle.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good sign that he asked. Reception can mark the review as only if he is not better, and keep him in light cotton, no heavy blanket. We will stop here.

spec.situation: Parent brings a toddler or school-age child with fever and cough; the two parents (or parent and grandparent) disagree about how long, how high, and what was given (paracetamol vs ibuprofen, doses by 'spoon'). Child says only a few words.
features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
